stem: A four-hour refactor across 60 files is approaching the context limit and Claude Code will auto-compact shortly. The migration plan and the list of already-converted files exist only in the conversation. What should happen first?

options.label: A
options.body: Write the plan and the converted list to a scratchpad file on disk, then re-read it afterwards.
options.rationale: Correct. Compaction is lossy by design — it keeps the gist and drops detail. State that must survive it belongs outside the transcript, on disk, where it can be read back verbatim into the fresh context.

options.label: B
options.body: Ask for a summary of the session so far and trust compaction to carry the important parts of that summary forward into the new context window.
options.rationale: A summary is exactly what compaction already produces, and it is where per-file detail gets lost. Summarising twice does not make the file list survive.

options.label: C
options.body: Raise the context limit so that compaction is deferred until the refactor across all 60 files is finished.
options.rationale: This postpones the problem rather than solving it, and the limit is not an arbitrary dial. A four-hour task will outgrow any window.

options.label: D
options.body: Start a fresh session and re-derive the remaining work by diffing the working branch against main before continuing.
options.rationale: A diff shows which files changed but not why, nor the ordering the plan depended on. It also throws away reasoning that was expensive to produce.

stem: Every new Claude Code session on the same monorepo spends its first ten minutes rediscovering the identical directory layout and build entry points. What is the durable fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Commit a short repo manifest describing layout and entry points, and reference it from CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: Correct. A committed manifest turns repeated exploration into a single cheap read, and referencing it from CLAUDE.md means every session loads it without anyone remembering to.

options.label: B
options.body: Keep one very long-lived session open across the whole week so that the exploration only ever has to be paid for once by the team.
options.rationale: A week-long session hits context limits and compaction repeatedly, and it cannot be shared across engineers working in parallel.

options.label: C
options.body: Have each engineer paste a description of the layout at the start of every session they open.
options.rationale: This works but relies on discipline and drifts out of date per person. Committing it once puts a single version under review.

options.label: D
options.body: Rely on `--resume` to carry the previous session's exploration into each new task that starts.
options.rationale: Resume continues one specific session; it does not give a new task, or another engineer, a shared map of the repository.

stem: Ninety minutes into a refactor, Claude reintroduces a callback pattern the team banned at the top of the conversation. Restating the ban fixes the file in hand, then the drift returns. What is the durable fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Move the ban into CLAUDE.md so it is reloaded as a standing rule instead of living in the transcript.
options.rationale: Correct. An instruction given once sits far back in a long conversation and competes with everything after it. Configuration is re-supplied on every turn, so it does not decay.

options.label: B
options.body: Restate the constraint in every single prompt from here on, since the most recent instruction always carries the most weight with the model.
options.rationale: It works turn by turn but puts the burden on the operator, and one forgotten restatement brings the drift straight back.

options.label: C
options.body: Shorten sessions so the constraint never falls far enough back to be lost.
options.rationale: This bounds the symptom rather than removing it, and it fragments work that genuinely needs a long session.

options.label: D
options.body: Ask the model to summarise the constraints agreed so far and then work from that summary for the rest of the session.
options.rationale: The summary itself ages the same way the original instruction did, and summarising is where precise wording tends to be lost.

stem: A ticket reads only "clean up the auth module." It could mean deleting dead code, splitting an oversized file, or swapping the session library — three very different diffs. What is the best first move?

options.label: A
options.body: Use plan mode to lay out the readings and get one confirmed before any file is edited.
options.rationale: Correct. The ambiguity is genuine and cheap to resolve up front, and expensive to resolve after a large diff exists. Plan mode is the built-in way to surface the choice without touching the tree.

options.label: B
options.body: Pick the reading with the smallest blast radius and begin there, on the grounds that a small diff is straightforward to revert later if it turns out to be the wrong one.
options.rationale: Guessing quietly is still guessing. Reverting costs the author's time and the reviewer's, and the ambiguity remains unresolved for the next ticket.

options.label: C
options.body: Implement all three readings on one branch so the reviewer can keep whichever was actually meant.
options.rationale: This triples the work and hands the reviewer a diff that cannot be assessed as a whole. Cost scales with the ambiguity instead of eliminating it.

options.label: D
options.body: Begin editing straight away and let the reviewer redirect at pull-request time, since scope is settled during review anyway.
options.rationale: Review is the most expensive place to discover a misread requirement, and it wastes the whole implementation.

stem: A team merges around 200 Claude-generated diffs a week and has the capacity to human-review about 30 of them. Which selection rule prevents the most damage?

options.label: A
options.body: Review everything touching auth, payments, or migrations first, then sample what is left.
options.rationale: Correct. Stratify by blast radius, not by volume. A defect in a migration or an auth path is unrecoverable in a way that a defect in a log message is not.

options.label: B
options.body: Review the 30 largest diffs measured by line count, on the reasoning that a bigger change carries proportionally more risk of containing a defect.
options.rationale: Line count tracks effort, not consequence. A three-line change to a permission check outranks a 400-line rename.

options.label: C
options.body: Review a uniform random 15% sample so every diff has an identical chance of being seen by a person.
options.rationale: Uniform sampling estimates an overall defect rate well but deliberately ignores severity, so it under-covers the few places that matter most.

options.label: D
options.body: Review the 30 the model itself rated lowest-confidence and treat its own confidence as sufficient for all the rest.
options.rationale: Self-reported confidence is a useful input but is itself unvalidated, and it is blind to which files are dangerous to get wrong.

stem: Claude is generating API documentation from the source code plus an older design document. For one endpoint the two disagree on the default timeout. What should the generated page do?

options.label: A
options.body: Give both values, each attributed to where it came from, and flag the conflict for a human.
options.rationale: Correct. The conflict is information. Attributing each figure preserves provenance and puts the decision with whoever can actually say which is authoritative.

options.label: B
options.body: Take the value from the source code, because running code is always more current than a design document and the older figure can simply be dropped.
options.rationale: Often true but not reliably so — the code may hold the bug the design document describes correctly. Silently picking one hides the disagreement.

options.label: C
options.body: Take the design document's value, since it records the contract the code is meant to implement.
options.rationale: This documents an intention rather than the behaviour callers will actually observe, and still conceals the conflict.

options.label: D
options.body: Leave the timeout out of the page until somebody reconciles the two inputs and confirms which figure is correct.
options.rationale: Omission loses the finding entirely — nobody learns there was a conflict, so nothing prompts the reconciliation.
